# Inspection Authorization (IA) qualifications as they relate to major alterations — 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D

**Short answer.** The *qualifications* to obtain an inspection authorization are in **14 CFR § 65.91**, specifically **§ 65.91(c)(1) through (5)**. The provision that governs what an IA may do *with a major alteration* is **§ 65.95(a)(1)** — that is a privilege/limitation rule, not a qualification rule. There is **no separate 'major alteration qualification'** in Part 65; the major-alteration content enters the IA scheme in exactly two places: (a) the eligibility test in § 65.91(c)(5) must examine the applicant's ability to inspect for return to service *after major repairs and major alterations*, and (b) the privilege in § 65.95(a)(1) to inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration.

*Scope note (Regulatory Engineer function):* this is a citation-and-rule-text deliverable — the regulation as published, with cross-references. It is not a legal opinion, an FAA enforcement interpretation, or a determination for a specific certificate holder; those come from the responsible Flight Standards office or FAA counsel.

---

## 1. The qualification rule — § 65.91(c), verbatim

> **(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—**
> **(1)** Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> **(2)** Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> **(3)** Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> **(4)** Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> **(5)** Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.

Source: eCFR, 14 CFR § 65.91 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.91 (retrieved 2026-11-15; quoted text matches the fetched page).

§ 65.91 also contains the application mechanics (application made on the form and in the manner the Administrator prescribes) and the holder's duty to keep the FAA informed of changes affecting eligibility; the eligibility substance, however, is (c)(1)–(5) above.

## 2. The major-alteration privilege — § 65.95(a), verbatim

> **(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—**
> **(1)** Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
> **(2)** Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter;

Source: eCFR, 14 CFR § 65.95 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95 (retrieved 2026-11-15; quoted text matches the fetched page).

FAA's own IA guidance states the same division of labor: "The basic functions of the holder of an inspection authorization (IA) are set forth in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 65, § 65.95. With the exception of aircraft maintained in accordance with a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program under part 121, an IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration." (FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide*, https://www.faa.gov/training_testing/testing/ia_info_guide.pdf.)

## 3. How each qualification maps to major alterations

| § 65.91(c) element | Requirement | Bearing on major alterations |
|---|---|---|
| (1) | Mechanic certificate, Airframe **and** Powerplant ratings, each current and in effect a total of at least 3 years | The IA is an *add-on* to a current A&P; you cannot hold an IA on the strength of one rating. Both airframe and powerplant scope is needed because major alterations can be airframe, powerplant, propeller, or appliance work (§ 65.95(a)(1) covers "any aircraft or related part or appliance"). |
| (2) | Actively engaged at least the 2-year period before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | Recent, in-regulatory-framework maintenance experience — the practical basis for judging whether an alteration conforms to approved data and Part 43. |
| (3) | Fixed base of operations, reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week (need not be where authority is exercised) | Administrative/eligibility element; it is where the FAA reaches the IA. It does not limit where the IA may inspect an alteration. |
| (4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | This is the direct hook to alterations: approving an alteration requires the inspection data (the approved technical data referenced in § 65.95(a)(1)) and the means to inspect the altered article. |
| (5) | Pass a written test on ability to inspect to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 | The only place in the *eligibility* rule where major alterations are named. The IA test is the competency gate for alteration approval. |

## 4. What is *not* a qualification (frequent misreads)

1. **§ 65.95 is not the eligibility rule.** It does not say who may obtain an IA; it says what an IA holder may do. Answering the qualification question with § 65.95 is a category error.
2. **No separate 'major alteration authorization' or endorsement exists** in Part 65 Subpart D. The single IA credential carries the § 65.95(a)(1) privilege.
3. **"Technical data approved by the Administrator" is a condition on the privilege, not a qualification on the person.** Under § 65.95(a)(1) the IA may approve for return to service only if the alteration work was done in accordance with Administrator-approved technical data. No approved data, no IA return-to-service approval — regardless of the IA's personal qualifications.
4. **Holding an IA is not required to *perform* an alteration.** Alteration work is authorized under § 43.3 (persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations); the IA's distinct role is *inspection and approval for return to service* under § 65.95(a)(1), read with the return-to-service rules of Part 43 (§ 43.5, § 43.7) and the record-entry requirement of § 43.9.
5. **Part 121 carve-out.** An IA may not use § 65.95(a)(1) on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program; those approvals run through the certificate holder's program.

## 5. Adjacent rules an IA must satisfy to keep exercising the privilege

- **Duration / renewal (§ 65.92, § 65.93).** An IA is time-limited, and renewal requires evidence that the holder *still* meets § 65.91(c)(1)–(4) — the FAA IA Information Guide frames renewal exactly that way ("Evidence the applicant still meets the requirements of 14 CFR § 65.91(c)(1) through (4)") — plus the recent-activity or refresher options that § 65.93 specifies. **Action item for the user:** read the current activity counts and refresher-hour figure directly at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.93 before relying on them; I did not re-verify those specific numbers in this pass and therefore do not state them here.
- **Definition of the trigger term.** "Major alteration" is defined in **14 CFR § 1.1** (an alteration not listed in the aircraft/engine/propeller specifications that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other airworthiness qualities, or that is not done by accepted practices/elementary operations) and enumerated in **Part 43, Appendix A**. Whether a given change is a *major* alteration determines whether § 65.95(a)(1) approval is required at all.
- **Performance and records.** Part 43 governs how the alteration is performed and recorded (§ 43.3 authorization, § 43.5/§ 43.7 return-to-service approval paths, § 43.9 maintenance record content, § 43.13 performance standards).
- **Related-but-distinct authorities.** A Part 145 repair station approving work within its ratings, a Designated Airworthiness Representative, and an Aviation Safety Inspector are separate return-to-service paths; the IA is the individual-mechanic path and is not a substitute for those approvals where the rules assign the function elsewhere.

## 6. Citation list (eCFR is authoritative per the request)

- 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D — Inspection Authorizations: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D
- § 65.91 Inspection authorization (eligibility, incl. (c)(1)–(5)): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.91
- § 65.95 Inspection authorization: privileges and limitations: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95
- § 65.92, § 65.93 (duration, renewal): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.92 , https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.93
- § 1.1 definitions (major alteration): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-1.1
- Part 43 and Appendix A (major alteration list; performance, return to service, records): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/part-43
- FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide*: https://www.faa.gov/training_testing/testing/ia_info_guide.pdf

**Currency:** text quoted is the eCFR "current" version as retrieved 2026-11-15. Re-pull the eCFR links above if the answer must be pinned to a later date or to a historical revision.

## 7. One-line takeaway for the AMT context

An A&P mechanic becomes eligible for the IA — and therefore for the § 65.95(a)(1) authority to inspect and approve for return to service after a major alteration — by meeting § 65.91(c)(1)–(5): current A&P held at least 3 years, at least 2 years of active engagement in maintaining 14 CFR–certificated aircraft, a fixed base of operations, the equipment/facilities/inspection data to do the job, and a passing score on the IA written test that specifically covers return to service after major repairs and major alterations.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION CD-2026-IA-MAJALT-01
Subject: Qualifications for an Inspection Authorization (IA) to inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft after a major alteration
Audience: FAA-certificated aviation maintenance technician (AMT) / mechanic certificate holder under 14 CFR Part 65
Jurisdiction: United States, Title 14 CFR. Source baseline: eCFR current text (retrieval baseline 2026-11-15, hashes in Section 11).
Prepared by: Compliance Engineer. Status: Issued for use, subject to the verification register in Section 10.

====================================================================
1. SCOPE, ASSUMPTIONS, AND WHAT IS OUT OF SCOPE
====================================================================
1.1 In scope
  (a) Eligibility to HOLD an inspection authorization: 14 CFR 65.91, 65.92, 65.93.
  (b) Authority to EXERCISE an inspection authorization on a major alteration: 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1).
  (c) The return-to-service and record-keeping obligations that attach when the IA signs: 14 CFR 43.5, 43.9, 43.13; 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A (major alteration definition).
1.2 Assumptions (state them if you reuse this memo)
  A1. 'FAA-AMT' = holder of a mechanic certificate under 14 CFR Part 65.
  A2. 'Inspection auth' = Inspection Authorization, not the generic conformity/field-approval inspection process.
  A3. 'Major alteration' is as defined in 14 CFR 1.1 and exemplified in Part 43 Appendix A.
  A4. Current regulation text is wanted, not the text in force at the time of an historical alteration.
  A5. U.S. federal rules apply; no foreign CAA, no military airworthiness rules.
1.3 Out of scope (route elsewhere if raised)
  - Part 121 continuous airworthiness maintenance program internal approval structures (see 121.379).
  - Repair station approval authority under Part 145.
  - DER/DAS data approval mechanics under Part 183 (referenced only as an approval-basis option in Section 6).
  - Practical test standards, training syllabi, and IA refresher course content.

====================================================================
2. DETERMINATION (SHORT FORM)
====================================================================
An AMT may inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or related part after a MAJOR ALTERATION only when ALL FOUR conditions below are satisfied. They are cumulative; failure of any one voids the approval.

  C1. BASE QUALIFICATION - the person holds a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective, that has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years (65.91(c)(1)).
  C2. CURRENT AUTHORIZATION - the person holds a currently effective inspection authorization, and it is being exercised only while the underlying mechanic certificate and both ratings remain effective (65.91; 65.92).
  C3. AIRCRAFT NOT EXCLUDED - the aircraft is NOT maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121 (express exclusion in 65.95(a)(1)).
  C4. APPROVED DATA - the alteration was accomplished in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator (65.95(a)(1)). The IA inspects for conformity to that data and approves for return to service; the IA does NOT approve the data itself.

Governing identifier: 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)-(5) (eligibility) and 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) (major-alteration privilege).

====================================================================
3. RULE MAP
====================================================================
 Section        Title / function                                              Role here
 ------------   ------------------------------------------------------------   --------------------------
 14 CFR 1.1     Definitions: major alteration / major repair                      Classify the change
 14 CFR 43.5    Approval for return to service after maintenance/alteration        What approval requires
 14 CFR 43.7    Persons authorized to approve for return to service                 Who may sign
 14 CFR 43.9    Content/form/disposition of maintenance & alteration records        Record entry
 14 CFR 43.13   Performance rules (methods, techniques, practices; quality)         Workmanship standard
 14 CFR 43 App A Major alteration/repair examples                                 Classification aid
 14 CFR 65.91   Inspection authorization: eligibility                              QUALIFICATIONS
 14 CFR 65.92   Inspection authorization: duration                                Currency
 14 CFR 65.93   Inspection authorization: renewal                                  Sustaining qualification
 14 CFR 65.95   Inspection authorization: privileges and limitations               AUTHORITY
 14 CFR 91.407  Operation after maintenance/alteration (return-to-service + check) Operating consequence
 14 CFR 91.417  Aircraft maintenance records                                        Record retention

CITATION NOTE (correction to the working research): the IA sections have been referred to in working notes as 'Part 65 Subpart D.' Subpart D of Part 65 is the mechanic certificate sections; the inspection authorization sections are grouped separately. Cite by section number (65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95) and use the eCFR section-level URL form (title-14/section-65.xx) so the citation does not depend on subpart lettering. The quoted text of 65.95(a)(1) below is unaffected.

====================================================================
4. PART A - QUALIFICATIONS TO HOLD AN INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (14 CFR 65.91)
====================================================================
65.91(a): application is made on the form and in the manner the Administrator prescribes (in practice the FAA mechanic/IA application form; confirm the current form number with the FAA before filing).

65.91(c) sets the substantive eligibility qualifications. An applicant must:

 A-1. (c)(1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective, and each of which has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years.
      -> Airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanics are NOT eligible. A lapsed rating disqualifies. Evidence to hold: certificate, airman registry record, effective dates.

 A-2. (c)(2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before applying, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR.
      -> 'Actively engaged' is employment/practice evidence, not a paper credential. Evidence to hold: employer letters, work orders, 43.9 entries signed, training records covering the 24 months.

 A-3. (c)(3) Have a fixed base of operations at which the applicant can be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week. The base need not be where the IA privileges are exercised.
      -> Evidence: address of record, phone, employer facility letter.

 A-4. (c)(4) Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
      -> This is a continuing capability, not a one-time application item: if the equipment/facilities/data are not available at the moment of exercise, the basis for exercising the privilege is not met. Evidence: tool list, calibrated equipment records, data subscription (maintenance manuals, AD service, type data).

 A-5. (c)(5) Pass a written test on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and for annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43.
      -> Note the test scope expressly names major alterations. Evidence: test completion record.

SUSTAINING QUALIFICATIONS
 S-1. 65.92 - the authorization runs on a 2-year cycle and expires on 31 March of each odd-numbered year; the holder may exercise the privileges only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating.
 S-2. 65.93 - renewal. Renewal requires continuing to meet the eligibility conditions and demonstrating recent inspection activity or an accepted alternative. The specific activity counts and alternatives in 65.93 are NOT restated here because they could not be verified against the fetched text; read 65.93 in the live eCFR and record the applicable option in the file. Do not rely on a remembered number.

KEY POINT: the IA is not a rating on the mechanic certificate and is not issued by anyone other than the FAA. There is no 'IA-endorsed' substitute for the certificate itself.

====================================================================
5. PART B - QUALIFICATIONS TO EXERCISE THE IA ON A MAJOR ALTERATION (14 CFR 65.95(a)(1))
====================================================================
Verbatim controlling text (eCFR, retrieved 2026-11-15):

  '(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may-
   (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
   (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to Sec. Sec. 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.'

Decompose (a)(1) into the four cumulative conditions of Section 2:
 B-1. 'The holder of an inspection authorization' -> C2. The IA must be currently effective at the moment of approval, and per 65.92 the underlying A&P with both ratings must also be currently effective. An expired IA cannot be revived by the supervisor's sign-off or by a later renewal.
 B-2. 'except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121' -> C3. For a Part 121 CAMP aircraft, the IA privilege does not exist. Route to the certificate holder's authorized approval process (compare 121.379). Note: the express exclusion names Part 121 only; do not extend or restrict it by assumption. Confirm the aircraft's actual maintenance program from the operator's manual/OpSpecs, not from the flight operation being conducted.
 B-3. 'after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43' -> the work must have been performed under Part 43 performance rules (43.13 methods/techniques/practices; work at least equal to original or properly altered condition).
 B-4. 'if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator' -> C4. This is the gating condition most often missed. See Section 6.

The IA's authority is CONFORMITY AND RETURN TO SERVICE. It is not authority to create, waive, or backfill approved data. If approved data does not exist, the IA cannot cure that by signing; the alteration must be routed to an approval path (Section 6.3).

====================================================================
6. PART C - 'TECHNICAL DATA APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR' (the C4 gate)
====================================================================
6.1 The IA must be able to point, in the file, to a specific approval basis covering the specific make/model/serial/configuration. Acceptable bases include:
   - Type certificate data, or a supplemental type certificate covering the alteration;
   - FAA field approval recorded on the repair/alteration form (FAA Form 337) for that specific alteration on that specific aircraft;
   - Data approved by an FAA designee holding the appropriate delegation (Part 183) and issued on the corresponding FAA data-approval form;
   - Airworthiness directives and the FAA-approved data they mandate;
   - Manufacturer/vendor instructions that the FAA has expressly approved for that alteration.
6.2 NOT approved data by itself: generic advisory circular material (e.g., AC 43.13-1B/2B accepted methods, techniques, and practices) and manufacturer's unapproved service information. These are 'acceptable data'; they support a major alteration only when the FAA has specifically approved their use for that alteration, or when the alteration is genuinely minor. Mislabeling acceptable data as approved data is the single most common finding in this area.
6.3 If no approved data exists: the alteration cannot be returned to service under 65.95(a)(1). Route to field approval (FAA), a designee data approval, or an STC before any return-to-service signature. Document the routing in the file.
6.4 The IA must confirm the approved data is the CURRENT revision and applies to the installed configuration (effectivity), not merely to the model family.

====================================================================
7. PART D - CONFORMANCE PROCEDURE / CHECKLIST
====================================================================
Run these steps in order; stop at the first failure.

 D-1  QUALIFY THE PERSON. Verify mechanic certificate with airframe AND powerplant ratings, both currently effective and in effect at least 3 years (65.91(c)(1)); verify the IA is currently effective and not past its 31 March odd-year expiration (65.92). Record certificate numbers and dates. [C1, C2]
 D-2  QUALIFY THE AIRCRAFT. Identify the maintenance program. If Part 121 CAMP -> IA privilege unavailable; escalate. [C3]
 D-3  CLASSIFY THE CHANGE. Determine major vs minor against 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A. Write down the specific criterion relied on. A misclassified minor alteration is a finding even if the paperwork is tidy.
 D-4  IDENTIFY THE APPROVED DATA. Record the approval basis, its identifier, revision, and effectivity (Section 6). If absent -> stop. [C4]
 D-5  VERIFY ACCOMPLISHMENT. Records review: work order, parts traceability, approved parts basis, 43.13(a)/(b) compliance, any deviation from data (a deviation is a new alteration requiring its own approval basis).
 D-6  PERFORM THE CONFORMITY INSPECTION. Physically verify the installation matches the approved data: dimensions, materials, fasteners, clearances, routing, sealing, torque, finishes, electrical load, systems interface.
 D-7  VERIFY WEIGHT AND BALANCE. Recompute/confirm; the alteration must not invalidate the W&B envelope. Record the result.
 D-8  VERIFY OPERATING LIMITATIONS AND FLIGHT MANUAL. If the alteration changes limitations or flight-manual data, confirm the revisions are made and set forth as required (43.5(a)(3); 91.9). Missing AFM supplement is a classic finding.
 D-9  OPERATIONAL CHECK. If the alteration may appreciably change flight characteristics or substantially affect operation in flight, confirm the required operational check/test flight is accomplished and logged (91.407(b); verify current paragraph text per Section 10).
 D-10 MAKE THE RECORD. Maintenance record entry with description of work or reference to acceptable data, date, performer, and the signature plus certificate number of the person approving for return to service (43.9(a)). Execute the repair/alteration form required by the Administrator for the major alteration (43.5(a)(2); FAA Form 337).
 D-11 APPROVE FOR RETURN TO SERVICE. Signature and certificate number. Confirm the approval is given only after D-6 through D-9 are complete - never in advance of inspection.
 D-12 FILE AND DISTRIBUTE. Retain the data package, conformity evidence, W&B, Form 337 copy, and records entries per the aircraft record requirements (91.417) and the current FAA guidance on Form 337 submission timing. Record the package location.

DECISION TREE (text form)
  Major alteration? --No--> treat as minor; Form 337 not required; still 43.9 record.
        |Yes
  Approved data exists? --No--> STOP: field approval / designee data approval / STC.
        |Yes
  Aircraft under Part 121 CAMP? --Yes--> STOP: IA privilege excluded; use operator's approval process.
        |No
  IA current AND A&P with both ratings current AND >=3 years? --No--> STOP: not eligible.
        |Yes
  Conformity inspection + W&B + limitations + operational check complete? --No--> STOP: do not sign.
        |Yes
  Sign 43.9 entry + Form 337; approve for return to service.

====================================================================
8. PART E - NON-COMPLIANCE FINDINGS TO TEST FOR
====================================================================
 E-1  Return-to-service signature on a major alteration with no Administrator-approved technical data (relying on AC 43.13 or manufacturer's unapproved instructions).
 E-2  Signature on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 CAMP.
 E-3  Privileges exercised while the mechanic certificate or either rating was not currently effective, or while the IA itself had expired.
 E-4  Airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic performing the 65.95(a)(1) approval.
 E-5  No conformity inspection actually performed; signature based on paperwork only.
 E-6  No Form 337, or Form 337 executed but not supported by the approval basis recorded in block 3 (or the equivalent data-approval entry).
 E-7  Weight and balance not revised or not verified.
 E-8  Flight manual supplement / operating limitations not revised where the alteration requires it (43.5(a)(3)).
 E-9  Alteration deliberately misclassified as minor to avoid field approval.

verdict.summary:
# FAA Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — Regulatory Answer

**Function:** Regulatory Specialist deliverable (U.S. FAA, Title 14 CFR)
**Primary sources:** eCFR Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D — Part 65 Subpart D (§§ 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95) and Part 43 (§§ 43.3, 43.5, 43.7, 43.9, 43.13, Appendix A); Part 1 § 1.1; Part 21 Subpart E.
**Currency of text:** as fetched from eCFR on 2026-11-15. Re-verify the amendment level at the cited URLs before relying on this for a compliance decision.

---

## 1. Short answer

The question (“what are the qualifications for inspection authorization regarding major alterations”) spans **two separate rules**. Both must be stated, or the answer is incomplete and legally wrong:

**(1) Eligibility to HOLD an inspection authorization — 14 CFR § 65.91(a).** An applicant must:
- hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** an Airframe rating and a Powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a **total of at least 3 years**;
- have been **actively engaged for at least the 2-year period** before applying in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the regulation;
- have a **fixed base of operations** at which the holder can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week (it need not be where the authorization is exercised);
- have available the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances;
- **pass the written test** on the ability to inspect to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations, and after annual and progressive inspections under Part 43.
- If the test is failed, **no retest for at least 90 days** (§ 65.91(b)).

**(2) Authority to use the IA on a major alteration — 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1).** The holder may inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or related part or appliance **after a major repair or major alteration only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, and **not** for an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.

**Critical framing:** § 43.7 is the **return-to-service authority** rule (who may sign), **not** an eligibility/qualifications standard. It names mechanic certificate holders and IA holders and then defers scope to Part 65. Do not cite § 43.7 as the qualifications rule.

---

## 2. Eligibility detail — § 65.91(a) (restated; confirm verbatim wording at eCFR § 65.91)

| # | Requirement | Test the applicant must satisfy | Evidence the FAA/FSDO will look for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 65.91(a)(1) | Mechanic certificate with Airframe **and** Powerplant ratings | Both ratings currently effective; each in effect a **total of at least 3 years** | Mechanic certificate number and issue dates |
| 65.91(a)(2) | Recent active engagement | **At least the 2 years immediately before application** actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated/maintained under 14 CFR | Employment/activity history, employer letters, work records |
| 65.91(a)(3) | Fixed base of operations | Reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week; need not be where the IA is exercised | Address/telephone of record |
| 65.91(a)(4) | Facilities and data | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, related parts/appliances | Description of facility and data subscription/library |
| 65.91(a)(5) | Written test | Pass the IA written test on inspecting to safety standards for return to service after major repairs/major alterations and after annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 | Test results |
| 65.91(b) | Retest floor | After a failure, **may not reapply for at least 90 days** | Test date |

Application is made to the FAA on the mechanic/IA application form (FAA Form 8610-1, Mechanic’s Application for Inspection Authorization — confirm current form number and submission channel with the local FSDO/IFO before filing).

---

## 3. Authority and conditions for major alterations — § 65.95(a)

**Verified text (eCFR, § 65.95(a)(1), fetched 2026-11-15):**

> “(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may— (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and”

**Verified text (eCFR, § 65.95(a)(2)):** the holder may perform an annual inspection, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection.

**Conditions distilled from § 65.95(a)(1) — all must be true before the IA signs:**

- **C1 — Valid IA.** The person holds a currently effective inspection authorization (§§ 65.91, 65.92). An expired IA confers no privileges.
- **C2 — Not a Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft.** The paragraph expressly excludes aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121.
- **C3 — The work is a major repair or major alteration** as determined under Part 1 § 1.1 and Appendix A to Part 43 (see § 4 below).
- **C4 — Accomplished in accordance with Part 43** (methods, techniques, practices and data per § 43.13; performance by authorized persons per § 43.3).
- **C5 — Done in accordance with technical data APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR.** “Acceptable” data (e.g., AC 43.13-1B/2B generic methods, unless specifically approved for the installation) is not sufficient for a major alteration. See § 5 below.
- **C6 — Records and form executed before return to service.** Maintenance record entry under § 43.9, and the repair/alteration form condition of § 43.5 (FAA Form 337, executed in the manner prescribed by the Administrator).

---

## 4. Major vs. minor — the threshold that triggers § 65.95(a)(1)

- **§ 1.1 definition.** *Major alteration* means an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. *Major repair* is defined in parallel terms.
- **Appendix A to Part 43** enumerates major alterations by category (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) and separately enumerates major repairs and preventive maintenance. Use Appendix A first; if the alteration is listed there, it is major regardless of the installer’s view.
- If the alteration is **not** listed in Appendix A **and** does not meet the § 1.1 appreciable-effect / non-elementary-operations test, it is **minor**, and § 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative authority — it is approved for return to service under the ordinary mechanic-certificate route of § 43.7(b) as scoped by Part 65.
- Practical rule for the AMT: the major/minor call must be made **and documented** before work begins, because it determines whether approved data must be obtained and who may sign the return to service.

---

## 5. What “technical data approved by the Administrator” means in practice

The IA does **not** approve design data. The IA approves the article for **return to service** after work already accomplished under data the FAA has approved. Approved data for an alteration typically comes from one of:

- Type certificate data / amended TC, or a **supplemental type certificate** under Part 21 Subpart E;
- **Parts Manufacturer Approval** parts and articles, TSO articles, and installations covered by them;
- **Airworthiness Directives** (mandatory data);
- Manufacturer service documents **only where the FAA has approved them** for the specific alteration;
- **FAA field approval** of the data for the specific alteration, processed per AC 43-210A (Standardized Procedures for Requesting Approval of Data for Major Repairs and Major Alterations) and FAA Order 8900.1 Volume 4, Chapter 9 — the ASI approves the data; the IA then approves the article for return to service.

Consequence: if a major alteration was accomplished on data that is merely “acceptable” and never approved, the IA **cannot** cure that by signing. The data must be approved (retrospectively via field approval where the FAA permits) before any return-to-service approval is defensible.

---

## 6. Records the IA must see/complete

- **§ 43.9(a)** — maintenance record entry containing (1) a description of the work, or reference to acceptable data; (2) the date of completion; (3) the name of the person performing the work; and (4) the signature and certificate number of the person approving the work for return to service. For a major alteration the description must be sufficient to identify the alteration and the approved data relied on.
- **§ 43.5** — no person may approve for return to service an aircraft or part that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless (1) the § 43.9/§ 43.11 record entry has been made; (2) the repair or alteration form authorized or furnished by the Administrator (FAA Form 337) has been executed in the prescribed manner; and (3) if operating limitations or approved flight manual data change, those limitations/data are revised per § 91.9.
- **Form 337 handling** — prepared in duplicate for a major repair/major alteration; one copy to the aircraft owner/operator and one transmitted to the FAA as directed. Confirm the current filing channel (FAA Form 337 submission route) at the time of use.
- **Operator records** — for Part 91 operators, retention of records of major alterations is governed by § 91.417; the IA should verify the operator’s record set is complete, not merely that the shop copy exists.

---

## 7. Duration, renewal and currency — §§ 65.92, 65.93

- **Duration (§ 65.92).** An inspection authorization is time-limited and expires on **March 31 of the first odd-numbered year after issuance** — i.e., a two-year cycle keyed to odd-numbered years. (Confirm verbatim at eCFR § 65.92.)
- **Renewal (§ 65.93).** Renewal for the next two-year cycle requires an application and evidence of recent activity within the lookback window — the regulation provides several alternative activity categories (annual inspections performed; major repairs/major alterations performed; progressive inspections performed or supervised; and an FAA-accepted refresher/currency route). **Paragraph-level verification note:** the exact enumerated list and the exact lookback wording in § 65.93 must be read from the current eCFR text before being quoted to a client or used in an exam answer; this memo states the structure of the rule, not a verbatim reproduction of § 65.93.
- **Currency point for major alterations:** the 24-month activity lookback for renewal counts **major repairs or major alterations performed** as one qualifying category — so an IA who does alteration work is also maintaining renewal currency. Do not conflate the renewal lookback with the § 65.91(a)(2) pre-application engagement requirement; they are different tests at different career stages.

---

## 8. What an IA may NOT do with a major alteration

1. **May not approve for return to service an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program** (§ 65.95(a)(1) express carve-out).
2. **May not approve design data.** The IA approves return to service; data approval is an FAA (or design-approval holder) function.
3. **May not sign off a major alteration done on unapproved data** (fails the § 65.95(a)(1) condition).
4. **May not sign off work not performed in accordance with Part 43** (e.g., unqualified performer under § 43.3, or methods/data violating § 43.13).
5. **May not exercise any IA privilege while the authorization is expired, surrendered, suspended, or revoked** (§ 65.92; §§ 65.91–65.95).
6. **Does not gain authority to perform the alteration itself from the IA.** Performance authority comes from § 43.3 and the mechanic certificate; the IA is an inspection/approval authority.
7. **Personal-inspection expectation.** FAA interpretive practice is that the IA must personally perform the inspection on which the approval rests; an IA cannot delegate the inspection and sign on someone else’s findings. Treat this as interpretive guidance (FAA legal interpretations / AC material), not as quoted regulatory text.

---

## 9. Procedure — IA approving a major alteration for return to service

1. **Classify the work.** Check Appendix A to Part 43; if not listed, apply § 1.1 (appreciable effect / elementary operations). Record the major/minor determination.
2. **Identify the approved data.** Confirm an STC, amended TC, PMA/TSO basis, AD, FAA-approved manufacturer document, or an FAA field approval covers the specific installation. Obtain the document, including revision level.
3. **Verify performance authority.** Confirm the persons who did the work were authorized under § 43.3 and used methods/techniques/practices and data per § 43.13.
4. **Verify IA validity.** Confirm the IA is currently effective and not expired under § 65.92, and that the aircraft is not a Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft.
5. **Personally inspect.** Conduct the inspection against the approved data: conformity to the data, workmanship, weight and balance impact, structural integrity, systems interface, and any operating-limitation or AFM changes.
6. **Resolve discrepancies before signing.** Any deviation from approved data is either corrected or becomes a new data-approval problem — it is not signed as-is.
7. **Make the § 43.9 record entry**, including the description/reference to approved data, date, performer, and the IA’s signature and certificate number.
8. **Execute FAA Form 337** in the prescribed manner and distribute per § 43.5 and current FAA filing instructions; revise operating limitations/AFM data per § 91.9 where the alteration changes them.
9. **Return to service** only after steps 1–8 are complete. Approval for return to service is the last act, not the first.
10. **Retain/verify records** consistent with § 91.417 (operator) and shop record-retention practice.

---

## 10. Frequent errors this answer is designed to prevent

| Error | Correction |
|---|---|
| Citing § 43.7 as the “qualifications” for an IA | § 43.7 is the return-to-service **authority** rule; qualifications are § 65.91 |
| Quoting only § 65.95 and omitting § 65.91 | The question asks for qualifications; § 65.91 supplies them, § 65.95 supplies the major-alteration authority |
| Approving a major alteration done on AC 43.13-1B “acceptable” methods | § 65.95(a)(1) requires **Administrator-approved** technical data |
| Overlooking the Part 121 continuous airworthiness carve-out | It is written into § 65.95(a)(1) |
| Treating the FAA-H-8083-30/-31 AMT handbooks as law | They are guidance; the regulation is Parts 1, 21, 43, 65, 91 |
| Forgetting Form 337 | § 43.5 conditions return to service on execution of the Administrator’s repair/alteration form |
| Using an expired IA | § 65.92 duration; no privileges after expiration |

verdict.summary:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) Qualifications as They Relate to Major Alterations

Source of record: eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D (Mechanics) — §§ 65.91, 65.93, 65.95, as fetched for this analysis (fetch timestamps 2026-11-15T04:20:05Z per the source log). Guidance supplement (not regulation): FAA *Inspection Authorization (IA) Information Guide*, faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf.

## 1. Direct answer

There is **no separate FAA qualification, endorsement, or rating for "major alterations."** A certificated airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanic becomes qualified to approve major alterations for return to service by holding an **inspection authorization** issued under **14 CFR § 65.91**. The controlling qualification text is **§ 65.91(c)**, and major alterations appear in the rule at exactly three points:

| # | Where major alterations appear | Citation | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Written test must cover return to service after major repairs and major alterations | § 65.91(c)(5) | **Eligibility** (a qualification you must satisfy to get the IA) |
| 2 | IA may inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration | § 65.95(a)(1) | **Privilege** (what the qualification lets you do) |
| 3 | Renewal activity: at least two major repairs or major alterations per 90 days held | § 65.93(a)(2) | **Currency** (what keeps the qualification alive) |

An applicant who can read only one thing should read § 65.91(c)(5): the IA qualification is *tested on* major alterations, and § 65.95(a)(1) is what the qualification then *authorizes*.

## 2. The qualifications, verbatim — 14 CFR § 65.91(c)

> "(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter."

That is the complete set. All five must be met; they are conjunctive ("must—"). There is no sixth condition keyed to major alterations.

## 3. Requirement-by-requirement reading, with the major-alteration bearing of each

| Para. | Requirement | Threshold / standard | Bearing on major alterations |
|---|---|---|---|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate with **both** airframe and powerplant ratings, currently effective | Each rating in effect for a **total of at least 3 years** | The IA is an authorization layered on an A&P certificate; there is no IA path for a mechanic holding only one rating. Major alterations to airframes and to powerplants both fall inside the privilege, so both ratings are prerequisites. |
| (c)(2) | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | Continuous **2-year period immediately before application** | General maintenance-experience gate; not major-alteration-specific. |
| (c)(3) | Fixed base of operations, locatable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | Base need **not** be where the authority is exercised | Supports the field-approval nature of major-alteration return-to-service. |
| (c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available | Must be adequate to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | Directly relevant: approving a major alteration for return to service requires the inspection data (approved technical data) to compare the work against. |
| (c)(5) | **Written test** on ability to inspect to safety standards for return to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | Pass the test | This is the only place in § 65.91 where major alterations are named. The qualification for major alterations is therefore *demonstrated knowledge of Part 43 return-to-service standards for major repairs and major alterations*, tested in writing. |

## 4. What the qualification authorizes for major alterations — 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1)

> "(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"

Three conditions are embedded in that privilege and each is a compliance check, not a formality:

1. **Scope exclusion** — the aircraft must not be maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121.
2. **Part 43 compliance** — the inspection and approval must be done in accordance with Part 43 (records, performance rules, return-to-service rules).
3. **Approved technical data** — the alteration itself must have been accomplished in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. An IA cannot approve a major alteration performed on unapproved data; that is a limit on the qualification's reach, not on the holder's competence.

Consequence for a mechanic **without** an IA: an A&P may *perform* a major alteration but is not the person who approves it for return to service; that approval is the IA (or repair station / other authorized person) function. (The return-to-service authorization rule is 14 CFR § 43.5 — cited here as a cross-reference; its exact text was not re-fetched in this pass and should be confirmed before being quoted in a compliance document.)

## 5. Keeping the qualification — 14 CFR § 65.93(a)

The qualification is not permanent. Quoted text:

> "(a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4).
> In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities during the second year of the 2-year period:
> (1) Performed at least one annual inspection for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or
> (2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or"

Operational reading for a major-alteration-heavy practice:
- Renewal is on a **2-year** cycle, evidenced in **March of each odd-numbered year** at the responsible Flight Standards office.
- The applicant must still meet **§ 65.91(c)(1) through (4)** — note that (c)(5) (the test) is not re-tested; it is a one-time eligibility condition.
- One qualifying activity must be shown **by March 31 of the first year** of the 2-year period, and one during the **second year**.
- **§ 65.93(a)(2)** is the major-alteration currency route: **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the authority was held. **§ 65.93(a)(1)** is the annual-inspection route at **one annual inspection per 90 days**. The two routes are alternatives; the rule says "or."
- Paragraphs (a)(3) through (5) of § 65.93 exist as further alternative activities; their exact text was not in the verified passage set for this pass and is deliberately not paraphrased here.

## 6. What counts as a "major alteration" — the applicability hinge

The qualifications in § 65.91(c) attach to the term "major alteration," so the definition governs whether the IA privilege is even engaged.
- **14 CFR § 1.1** defines a major alteration, in substance, as an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness, or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A** lists major alterations by category (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliances).
- Verification status: the § 1.1 and Appendix A texts above are standard-reference content and were **not** among the passages fetched for this analysis. Treat them as the correct citations to pull and confirm on eCFR before quoting in a formal compliance document; the § 65.91(c) / § 65.95(a)(1) / § 65.93(a) answer does not depend on them.

## 7. What is NOT required (frequently assumed, not in the rule)

- No separate "major alteration" endorsement, stamp, rating, or certificate beyond the inspection authorization itself.
- No type rating, no aircraft-specific authorization, and no minimum number of major alterations performed before *initial* issuance. Major-alteration volume appears only as a **renewal** activity option (§ 65.93(a)(2)), not as an initial eligibility criterion.
- No additional test beyond the § 65.91(c)(5) written test at initial issuance (no re-test at renewal — § 65.93(a) requires evidence of § 65.91(c)(1)-(4) plus activity only).
- The IA is an **authorization**, not a rating on the mechanic certificate; it does not expand the holder's maintenance privileges generally, only the inspection/approval privileges in § 65.95.

## 8. Eligibility checklist a competent engineer can run directly

For each IA applicant, record pass/fail with the evidence:

1. A&P certificate — both airframe and powerplant ratings, currently effective, each in effect a total of **≥ 3 years** → cite § 65.91(c)(1); evidence = certificate number and issue dates.
2. Active engagement in maintaining 14 CFR-certificated aircraft for the **2 years** immediately preceding application → § 65.91(c)(2); evidence = employment/work records.
3. Fixed base of operations with person-or-telephone reachability during a normal working week → § 65.91(c)(3); evidence = address and contact statement (note: base need not be where authority is exercised).
4. Equipment, facilities, and inspection data adequate to inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts/appliances → § 65.91(c)(4); evidence = facility/equipment list and data subscription (e.g., approved technical data access).
5. Written test passed, covering return-to-service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 → § 65.91(c)(5); evidence = test result.
6. Application made on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator → § 65.91(a) (application mechanics; confirm current form on FAA site).

For each IA **holder** exercising the privilege on a major alteration, record:

7. Aircraft not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program → § 65.95(a)(1) exclusion.
8. Alteration accomplished in accordance with **technical data approved by the Administrator** → § 65.95(a)(1) condition.
9. Inspection and approval performed in accordance with **Part 43** → § 65.95(a)(1).
10. Currency: renewal evidence in March of the odd-numbered year, § 65.91(c)(1)-(4) still met, plus an activity under § 65.93(a) in year one (by March 31) and in year two — e.g., **two major repairs or major alterations per 90 days held** under § 65.93(a)(2).

## 9. Currency and sourcing notes

- Regulation text above is the current eCFR text for 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D, as fetched for this analysis; § 65.91(c), § 65.93(a), and § 65.95(a)(1) are quoted from the fetched pages and can be relied on as quoted.
- Not verified in this pass, and therefore not quoted or paraphrased as rule text: § 65.91(a)/(b)/(d) application mechanics; § 65.92 (duration of an inspection authorization); the full § 65.95 privilege list beyond (a)(1); § 65.93(a)(3)-(5) and (d); § 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A definitions; § 43.5. Each is identified by citation so it can be pulled and confirmed on ecfr.gov before external use.
- FAA guidance (the IA Information Guide) and any Flight Standards office practice supplement the rule but do not create additional regulatory qualifications; where guidance and § 65.91(c) diverge, § 65.91(c) controls.
